title_options: Why Double Speed Means 4x Braking Distance 🚗
facts: Braking distance d = v^2 / (2a): at a steady deceleration it grows with the square of speed, so doubling speed quadruples it (school physics; Save My Exams GCSE notes; Brake road-safety charity).

Worked numbers for a hard stop on a dry road (deceleration about 7 m/s^2): 30 km/h (8.3 m/s) -> about 5 m; 60 km/h (16.7 m/s) -> about 20 m. UK Highway Code braking distances 14 m at 30 mph and 55 m at 60 mph show the same ~4x ratio.
Kinetic energy = 1/2 m v^2; the brakes turn it into heat. Thinking distance (reaction time) is extra.
description: Drive twice as fast and your car needs four times as far to stop. Here's the physics, with two cars braking side by side. #shorts #physics #science #cars
sources: Braking distance = speed^2 / (2 x deceleration), kinetic energy = 1/2 m v^2 (GCSE physics, e.g. Save My Exams); UK Highway Code braking distances (14 m at 30 mph, 55 m at 60 mph).

scenes.narration: Drive twice as fast, and your car needs four times as far to stop.
Both of these cars brake hard at the same line. One is doing thirty kilometres an hour, the other sixty.
On a dry road, the slow car stops in about five metres. The fast one needs about twenty.
That's because the brakes have to get rid of the car's moving energy, and that energy grows with speed squared.
Double the speed, and there's four times the energy to burn off as heat.
And that's before you add the moment it takes you to react.
So how much farther would a car doing ninety need to stop?
